blocks.content: Say you are building the map screen for a food delivery app. The user opens the app in Koramangala and wants to see every restaurant within a two kilometer box around them. You have three million restaurant locations in your database, spread across the whole country.

The naive move is to loop through all three million points and check which ones fall inside that box. That works, technically, but it is doing three million comparisons to answer a question about a tiny patch of the map. Most of those points are nowhere near Koramangala, and you are wasting almost all of that work.

A quad tree exists to fix exactly this kind of waste. It lets you organize two dimensional points so that a query like "give me everything inside this box" only ever touches the small part of the data that could possibly matter, and skips everything else without even looking at it.
1. Introduction

Quad trees show up anywhere you have points, or shapes, scattered across a two dimensional space and you need to repeatedly ask location based questions about them. Find everything near me. Find everything inside this rectangle. Find what a click on the screen actually hit.

A plain list of points cannot answer these questions efficiently. It has no idea which points are near each other in space, so every query degrades into a full scan. A quad tree bakes spatial proximity into the structure itself, so nearby points end up grouped together, and far away points can be ignored in bulk.
A quad tree is a tree where every node represents a square region of space, and a node splits into four equal children the moment it is holding too many points to search efficiently on its own.
That single idea, split into four when a region gets crowded, is the entire trick. Everything else in this lesson is just a consequence of that one rule.
2. What a Quad Tree Actually Is
blocks.text: 2. What a Quad Tree Actually Is

blocks.content: Picture a square map of your city taped to a wall. Now imagine folding that map in half, then in half again, so it is creased into four equal quadrants: top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right. That fold is literally what a quad tree does to space, except it only folds a region once that region actually has enough points crammed into it to be worth splitting.

Each node in the tree owns a rectangular region and a small bucket of points. As long as the bucket has room, the node just stores points directly, no splitting needed. The moment the bucket would overflow past some threshold, say four or eight points, the node splits its region into four equal quadrants and hands its points down to whichever child quadrant they physically fall inside.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305811873-181814549.png
blocks.alt: A square region splitting into four equal quadrants, NW, NE, SW, SE

blocks.content: 2.1 The four children: NW, NE, SW, SE
blocks.text: 2.1 The four children: NW, NE, SW, SE

blocks.content: Every internal node in a quad tree has exactly four children, one for each quadrant of its region: northwest, northeast, southwest, southeast. That is where the name comes from, quad as in four. Each child owns exactly one quarter of the parent's area, and the four children together tile the parent's region perfectly, with no gaps and no overlap.

A leaf node, one that has not split, just holds a small list of points directly. An internal node holds no points of its own anymore, it has already pushed all of them down into whichever of its four children they belong to.
2.2 When a cell actually splits

The threshold is a tuning knob, not a fixed law. A common choice is something like four points per node before splitting. Below that, a linear scan over four items is basically free, so there is no benefit to going deeper. Above it, splitting starts paying for itself because you get to skip three quarters of the region on the next query.

This threshold based splitting is exactly why a quad tree adapts its shape to your actual data. A crowded downtown area keeps splitting, block by block, until each tiny node has only a handful of points. A quiet stretch of highway with three gas stations spread across fifty kilometers might never split at all, it stays one big, coarse node because there was never a reason to cut it up.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305814942-701173785.png
blocks.alt: A dense downtown region splitting into four smaller cells while a sparse suburb region stays one coarse cell

blocks.title: Depth is data driven
blocks.content: A quad tree does not have a fixed depth. Dense regions of the map get many levels of subdivision, sparse regions get almost none. The tree shape mirrors where your data actually lives.
3. How Insertion Works

Inserting a new point is a walk down the tree, not a search through a list. You start at the root, and at each node you ask one simple question: does this node still have room, or has it already split.

["If the current node is a leaf with room left, just add the point to its bucket and stop.","If the current node is a leaf that is now full, split it into four quadrants, redistribute its existing points into the correct children, then continue inserting the new point into whichever child it falls into.","If the current node has already split, figure out which of the four quadrants the point's coordinates fall inside, and recurse into that child."]
items: If the current node is a leaf with room left, just add the point to its bucket and stop.

If the current node is a leaf that is now full, split it into four quadrants, redistribute its existing points into the correct children, then continue inserting the new point into whichever child it falls into.
If the current node has already split, figure out which of the four quadrants the point's coordinates fall inside, and recurse into that child.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396030999-683817205.png
blocks.alt: Insertion walking from the root, picking a matching quadrant, and either adding to a leaf with room or splitting first

blocks.content: 3.1 Walking down the tree

At every level, deciding which quadrant a point belongs to is just comparing its x and y coordinates against the midpoint of the current region. Left half or right half, top half or bottom half, those two comparisons tell you exactly which of the four children to recurse into. No searching, no scanning, just arithmetic.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305818801-206380738.png
blocks.alt: A root node with four children, one of which has split further into its own four grandchildren

blocks.content: Notice the tree only grows deeper where it needs to. A child that never gets more than four points sitting inside it stays a leaf forever, it never pays the cost of subdividing further. Depth only accumulates where points actually cluster.
4. How Range Queries Work

This is the entire payoff. Say your delivery app wants every restaurant inside a bounding box around the user. You start at the root and ask one question at every node: does this node's region overlap the query box at all.
If a node's region does not overlap the query box, none of the points anywhere underneath that node can possibly be inside the box either, so the whole subtree gets skipped in one comparison.
4.1 Skipping quadrants that cannot possibly match
blocks.text: 4.1 Skipping quadrants that cannot possibly match

blocks.content: This is where a quad tree earns its keep. At the root, instead of checking every point, you check four rectangles. Maybe only two of those four quadrants actually overlap the query box, so you throw away the other two immediately, along with everything inside them. Recurse into the two that do overlap and repeat the same trick at the next level down.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305820465-225399443.png
blocks.alt: A range query descending only into the NW and SE quadrants that overlap the search box, skipping NE and SW entirely

blocks.content: Each recursive call either bails out instantly because there is zero overlap, or it does a small amount of real work checking the handful of points in that node. The number of nodes actually visited scales with how much of the map your query box touches, not with how many points exist in the whole dataset.

blocks.title: Why this beats a flat list
blocks.content: A flat list of points has no notion of where anything is relative to anything else, so a range query over a list has to check every single point, every single time, no matter how small the query box is.
5. Quad Tree vs Linear Scan vs Geohash
blocks.text: 5. Quad Tree vs Linear Scan vs Geohash

blocks.content: Three different ways to answer the same question, find every point inside a region, and they make very different trade-offs.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305822144-828173262.png
blocks.alt: A linear scan running millions of comparisons next to a quad tree query running a few dozen comparisons for the same question

blocks.content: 5.1 The naive linear scan

Check every point, keep the ones inside the box. Dead simple to implement, zero setup cost, and it is genuinely fine for small datasets. It falls apart the moment you have millions of points and need this answer many times a second.
5.2 Geohash: fixed size cells

Geohash carves the whole world into a grid of fixed size cells and gives each cell a short string code. Points sharing a prefix are near each other, so you can find neighbors by comparing string prefixes. It is simple and works great when your data is spread out evenly.

The catch is that the cell size is fixed ahead of time and does not care where your points actually are. A geohash cell sized for a city block is huge and mostly empty out in the countryside, and a geohash cell sized for the countryside is way too coarse inside a crowded city center, you end up scanning far more points than you need to in the dense areas.
5.3 Quad tree: cell size adapts to density
blocks.text: 5.3 Quad tree: cell size adapts to density

blocks.content: A quad tree keeps splitting wherever points are dense and stops splitting wherever they are sparse, so cell size naturally shrinks in crowded areas and stays large in empty ones. You get fine grained precision exactly where it is needed and no wasted subdivision where it is not.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305823946-329564777.png
blocks.alt: Quad tree cells shrinking in dense areas and staying large in sparse areas, next to geohash cells that stay the same fixed size everywhere

Simple, but cost grows with total data size regardless of query size."],["Geohash","Fixed size cells everywhere. Simple string based lookups, but wastes work in dense areas and loses precision in sparse ones."],["Quad tree","Cell size adapts to local density. 6. Worked Example: Restaurants in a City
blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: Restaurants in a City

blocks.content: Let us make this concrete. You have three million restaurant locations across the country, each with a latitude and longitude. You build one quad tree rooted at the bounding box of the whole country, with a capacity of, say, eight restaurants per node before it splits.

blocks.title: Finding restaurants near Koramangala
blocks.text: The user's box covers roughly two kilometers around their pin. Starting at the root, which covers the entire country, you immediately see the box only overlaps a tiny sliver of the root's area. You recurse into just the one or two quadrants that actually touch that sliver, ignoring the rest of the country in a single check.

blocks.content: A few levels down, you reach quadrants sized roughly to a city district. Since Koramangala is a dense area, the tree has already split several more times right there, so the nodes you are now checking cover just a few blocks each. You keep recursing only into the ones overlapping the query box.

By the time you reach the leaves, you are looking at nodes covering a couple of streets, each holding a handful of restaurants. You check each of those restaurants against the exact box and return the matches. Total nodes visited: maybe a few dozen. Total restaurants actually compared one by one: maybe a hundred, out of three million.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305825665-575064787.png
blocks.alt: A bounding box query checking each quadrant for overlap, scanning the two matching ones, skipping the third, and returning restaurant matches

blocks.content: ["Start at the root, covering the whole country.","At each node, check whether its square overlaps the query box at all.","If it does not overlap, skip that entire branch, no matter how many restaurants live underneath it.","If it does overlap and has children, recurse into each of the four children.","If it does overlap and is a leaf, check each of its few restaurants directly against the box."]
items: Start at the root, covering the whole country.
At each node, check whether its square overlaps the query box at all.
If it does not overlap, skip that entire branch, no matter how many restaurants live underneath it.
If it does overlap and has children, recurse into each of the four children.
If it does overlap and is a leaf, check each of its few restaurants directly against the box.

blocks.content: Compare that to the linear scan version of the same query: three million distance checks, every single time a user opens the map. The quad tree version touches a number of nodes roughly proportional to how much of the map the query box actually covers, which for a two kilometer box in a country sized dataset is a tiny fraction of the whole tree.
7. Where Quad Trees Show Up in Real Systems
blocks.text: 7. Where Quad Trees Show Up in Real Systems

blocks.content: Quad trees are not just a database indexing trick, they show up in a handful of very different domains, all sharing the same underlying need: quickly answer questions about points or shapes scattered in two dimensional space.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305827440-759667757.png
blocks.alt: A quad tree feeding four different real world uses: game engines, mapping apps, collision detection, image compression

blocks.content: 7.1 Game engines

Game engines use quad trees to figure out which objects are near the player, or near each other, without checking every object in the world on every single frame. A large open world map gets carved up the same way a city map does, and only the handful of objects in nearby cells get considered for rendering or physics each frame.
7.2 Mapping applications

This is the restaurant example from earlier, generalized. Any map product, food delivery, ride hailing, real estate listings, needs to answer "what is near me" or "what is inside this visible map area" constantly, and a quad tree is a natural fit for indexing exactly that.
7.3 Collision detection

Before checking whether two objects actually collide, a game or simulation first needs to narrow down which pairs of objects are even close enough to possibly be touching. Checking every pair of objects against every other pair is quadratic and gets slow fast. A quad tree groups nearby objects together so you only run the expensive precise collision check on pairs that share a cell.
7.4 Image compression

An image is just a two dimensional grid of pixels, and a quad tree can represent it by splitting the image into four quadrants whenever a region has too much variation in color, and leaving flat, uniform regions as a single leaf storing one average color. Large flat areas of sky or background compress down to a single node, while detailed areas keep subdividing, similar in spirit to how JPEG breaks images into blocks.
8. Quad Trees in System Design Interviews
blocks.text: 8. Quad Trees in System Design Interviews

blocks.content: Quad trees tend to come up whenever an interview question involves anything location based: design a ride hailing dispatch system, design a food delivery map, design Uber, design a Yelp style nearby search. The moment you hear "find things near a location" at scale, spatial indexing is a relevant piece of the answer.

["Explain the problem first: a naive scan over every point does not scale once you have millions of locations and need sub second responses.","Introduce the quad tree as a way to prune most of the space away with just a handful of overlap checks.","Mention the threshold based splitting, so the interviewer knows you understand the tree shape adapts to data density, not a fixed grid.","Be ready to compare it against geohash, since many real systems, including some ride hailing platforms, actually use geohash for its simplicity and because it plays nicely with existing key value stores.","Mention that in a distributed system, you would likely shard the quad tree itself, or use a geohash prefix as the shard key, since a single quad tree living on one machine eventually becomes its own bottleneck."]
items: Explain the problem first: a naive scan over every point does not scale once you have millions of locations and need sub second responses.
Introduce the quad tree as a way to prune most of the space away with just a handful of overlap checks.
Mention the threshold based splitting, so the interviewer knows you understand the tree shape adapts to data density, not a fixed grid.

Be ready to compare it against geohash, since many real systems, including some ride hailing platforms, actually use geohash for its simplicity and because it plays nicely with existing key value stores.

Mention that in a distributed system, you would likely shard the quad tree itself, or use a geohash prefix as the shard key, since a single quad tree living on one machine eventually becomes its own bottleneck.

blocks.title: A quad tree is not always the right answer
blocks.content: If your data is roughly evenly distributed across the region, a fixed grid or geohash can be simpler to build, simpler to shard, and just as fast in practice. Reach for a quad tree specifically when your data is clustered unevenly and you want the index itself to adapt to that.
9. Trade-offs and Limitations
Nothing here is free. A quad tree buys you fast, targeted queries at the cost of extra bookkeeping and some tricky edge cases.
9.1 Handling deletes and moving points

Removing a point is easy on its own, find its leaf and drop it from the bucket. The harder part is deciding when to merge four now sparse children back into one node. Skip that cleanup and the tree accumulates a lot of nearly empty nodes over time, which slowly erodes the exact efficiency you built the structure for in the first place.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305828956-16785423.png
blocks.alt: A parent node checking whether its now nearly empty children should be merged back into one coarser node

blocks.content: 9.2 Points that sit exactly on a boundary
blocks.text: 9.2 Points that sit exactly on a boundary

blocks.content: A point sitting exactly on the line between two quadrants needs a consistent rule, always round toward one side, or it can end up double counted or missed depending on how the comparison is written. This sounds minor until you are debugging why a query near a boundary returns one fewer restaurant than it should.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305830572-777966142.png
blocks.alt: A point sitting exactly on a quadrant edge being assigned to one side by a consistent rounding rule

blocks.title: Pick a rule and never break it
blocks.content: Whatever tie breaking rule you choose for boundary points, apply it identically during insertion and during querying. A mismatch between the two is a classic source of quad tree bugs that only show up near cell edges.

10. Key Takeaways

["A quad tree recursively splits a 2D region into four equal quadrants whenever a node holds more points than its threshold allows.","Insertion walks down the tree, splitting a leaf only when it actually overflows.","Range queries only recurse into quadrants that overlap the query box, skipping the rest without inspecting a single point inside them.","Compared to a linear scan, a quad tree turns a full data scan into a small number of overlap checks plus a handful of real point comparisons.","Compared to geohash, a quad tree adapts its cell size to data density, while geohash uses a fixed cell size everywhere.","Real usage spans game engines, mapping applications, collision detection, and image compression."]
items: A quad tree recursively splits a 2D region into four equal quadrants whenever a node holds more points than its threshold allows.
Insertion walks down the tree, splitting a leaf only when it actually overflows.
Range queries only recurse into quadrants that overlap the query box, skipping the rest without inspecting a single point inside them.
Compared to a linear scan, a quad tree turns a full data scan into a small number of overlap checks plus a handful of real point comparisons.
Compared to geohash, a quad tree adapts its cell size to data density, while geohash uses a fixed cell size everywhere.
Real usage spans game engines, mapping applications, collision detection, and image compression.

blocks.content: A quad tree is just the fold the map, split when crowded rule, applied recursively, so your queries only ever look where the answer could actually be.

Once this clicks, spotting when to reach for a quad tree in a system design interview becomes a lot easier. Anytime you hear a question shaped like "find things near a location fast" at real scale, this is one of the first tools worth mentioning.
